column2: On the authority of Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī Jurthūm ibn Nāshir (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: “Allah the Exalted has laid down obligations, so do not neglect them;

He has set limits, so do not overstep them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; and He has remained silent about things out of mercy for you, not out of forgetfulness, so do not search into them.” A ḥasan hadith, reported by al-Dāraquṭnī and others.
Al-Nawawī graded the hadith ḥasan, and before him Abū Bakr ibn al-Samʿānī, as Ibn Rajab said. There is a break in its chain, but Ibn Rajab mentioned what supports its meaning,
saying (2/150–151): “The meaning of this hadith has been narrated as the Prophet's own words through other routes. Al-Bazzār recorded it in his Musnad, and al-Ḥākim, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ,
from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: ‘Whatever Allah has made lawful in His Book is lawful, whatever He has made unlawful is unlawful, and whatever He has remained silent about is pardoned;

so accept from Allah His pardon, for Allah would never forget anything.’ Then he recited this verse: ‘And your Lord is never forgetful’ [Maryam 19:64]. Al-Ḥākim said: Its chain is authentic; and al-Bazzār said: Its chain is sound.”
The ḥāfiẓ Ibn Rajab said in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (2/152–153): “In the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah he divided the rulings of Allah into four categories: obligations,

prohibitions, limits and what is passed over in silence; and that gathers all the rulings of the religion. Abū Bakr ibn al-Samʿānī said: This hadith is a great foundation among the foundations of the religion. He said:

It is reported that one of them said: There is no single hadith among the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that on its own gathers the foundations and branches of knowledge more than the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah. He said: And it is reported that Wāthilah al-Muzanī said:

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gathered the religion in four phrases—then he mentioned the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah. Ibn al-Samʿānī said: Whoever acts on this hadith has won the reward and is safe from punishment,

because whoever performs the obligations, avoids the prohibitions, stops at the limits and leaves searching into what has been kept from him has fulfilled all the categories of merit and given the religion its full rights,
for the laws do not go beyond these kinds mentioned in this hadith. End of quotation.”

His words, “Allah has laid down obligations, so do not neglect them”, mean: He has made things obligatory and made their obligation binding, such as prayer, zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj; every Muslim must perform them as Allah has commanded, without leaving them or falling short in doing them.

His words, “He has set limits, so do not overstep them”, mean: He has prescribed matters that are obligatory, recommended or permissible, so one should not go beyond those limits to something else and fall into what is unlawful. An example is the inheritance shares that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has set out in His Book;

no one may overstep them and make a division that contradicts them. “Limits” (ḥudūd) are also used to mean what Allah has made unlawful, in which case the Muslim must not go near them, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them” [al-Baqarah 2:187].

His words, “He has forbidden things, so do not violate them”, mean that Muslims may not fall into what Allah has made unlawful; rather, they must leave it, as he ﷺ said: “What I have forbidden you, avoid it.”

His words, “and He has remained silent about things out of mercy for you, not out of forgetfulness, so do not search into them”, mean: there are matters about which no text has come in the Book and the Sunnah,

so one should not occupy oneself with searching into them and asking about them, like the question about Ḥajj every year, for which the Messenger ﷺ rebuked the questioner, saying: “Leave me as long as I leave you,

for what destroyed those before you was only their excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets”; and like asking about the prohibition of something not prohibited, so that it becomes prohibited because of the question,
the danger of which is established in the hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. After his ﷺ time, one should not ask questions involving hair-splitting and affectation.
The meaning is that He remained silent about things, not making them obligatory or binding and not forbidding them, so they should not be asked about. Allah the Exalted said:

“O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qurʾān is being revealed, they will be made plain to you. Allah has pardoned it, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing. A people before you asked such questions and then became disbelievers on account of them” [al-Māʾidah 5:101–102].

Ibn Rajab said (2/163): “As for what is passed over in silence, it is that whose ruling is not mentioned, whether as permissible, obligatory or unlawful; it is pardoned, and there is no blame on the one who does it. This is what these hadiths mentioned here indicate, such as the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah and others.”
Part of Allah's Sharīʿah is binding obligation, which must be done and not neglected.
One must stop at the obligatory, the recommended and the permissible, and not go beyond them to the unlawful.
Everything Allah has made unlawful, the Muslim must leave and keep far from.
Whatever has neither prohibition nor permission concerning it is pardoned and is not to be asked about.
